name: Traxy
tagline: An AI-layered tracking tool: it captures a stream of activity and turns it into summaries, charts and nudges.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: We have not verified Traxy's exact feature set, so treat this as a read on the shape of the product rather than a line-by-line teardown. Anything that is fundamentally a tracker plus an LLM summary pass is a well-trodden weekend build: a table of entries, some aggregation math, a chart, and one prompt that turns the last 90 days into five bullet points. The part that does not fall out of a one-shot is data capture that you do not have to do by hand, which usually means OAuth against other people's APIs, plus a mobile app and push notifications for the nudges to matter. If the hosted product's real value is automatic ingestion from tools you already use, the DIY version degrades into a manual log you stop filling in by week three. If the value is mostly the dashboard and the AI commentary, you can own that outright.
coreLoopDIY: Logs whatever you tell it to log into a local SQLite file, computes streaks and trends, and runs one LLM pass over the recent history to produce plain-language observations.
requirements: Node 20+ and a local SQLite file
Optional LLM API key for the summary layer, with a deterministic stats fallback when it is missing
Discipline to log manually, or time to wire up whichever source API you actually care about
whatYouLose: Automatic data capture from third-party tools; your version starts as a manual log
A mobile app and real push notifications, which is where most tracking habits live or die
Cross-device sync without you standing up hosting and auth yourself
Whatever prompt tuning and report design they have iterated on with real users
Someone else fixing it when an upstream API changes
moatNotes: Trackers compete on how little the user has to type. Every integration you do not build is a reason the local version rots.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay tracking tools for the part that is boring to build and impossible to forget: an app on the phone, a notification at the right time, and data that arrives without being typed. The analytics and the AI commentary are the demo, not the moat. A self-built version nails the demo in a weekend and then quietly dies because nobody opens localhost:3000 at 11pm to log anything.
notes: The dashboard is a weekend; the habit of actually feeding it is the product.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal tracking app called mytrax in this empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite via better-sqlite3, Recharts for charts. Single user, runs on localhost with npm run dev. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics scripts.

Data model in SQLite with a migration file:
- tracker: id, name, kind (number | boolean | duration | text), unit, target, cadence (daily | weekly), archived
- entry: id, trackerId, value (stored as text, parsed by kind), note, occurredAt (ISO), createdAt
- tag and entryTag join table

Screens:
1. /today: one quick-add row per active tracker, keyboard-first, Enter saves and moves to the next tracker. Shows current streak per tracker.
2. /t/[id]: history table plus a line or bar chart, rolling 7 and 30 day averages, target line if set, inline edit and delete.
3. /insights: aggregate view across trackers plus an AI report section.

AI layer: POST /api/insight serializes the last 90 days of entries as compact CSV, sends it to the OpenAI API with a prompt asking for exactly five short observations about trends, correlations and gaps, and returns them as JSON. Read OPENAI_API_KEY from .env.local. If the key is missing or the call fails, render deterministic fallback stats (best streak, biggest week-over-week change, most missed tracker) instead of an error.

Also include: CSV import and full JSON export, a seed script with 120 days of plausible fake data, and vitest tests covering streak calculation, cadence bucketing and CSV parsing.

Explicitly out of scope: mobile app, push notifications, multi-user, OAuth, third-party integrations, billing, Docker.

Write a README with setup steps and a .env.example. Do not commit any secrets.
